messages.subject: corrupt GenomeInformation
messages.body_plain:
Group

I have a problem with the getGenomeInformation method for
GenomeWideSNP_6.

Here's what happened:
a) I had a nicely created cdf object
b) i had processed data using AvgCnPlm
c)  I had been trying to retireve the full annotation info so that I
could do some specialized copy number analysis in some custom regions

I decided to overwrite the getData.GenomeInformation method so that I
could get both the SNP ids and the Unit ids into the dataframe.

somehow in the midst of this process I seem to have 'broken' some
internal object, and now whenever I restart and try to invoke the
default method for :
gi <- getGenomeInformation(cdf,force=T);
result<-gi$getData()

result has only NA entries for chromosome and physicalPosition.

I have gone through the process of resinstalling both the
 GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,na24,HB20080214.ufl
GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,na24,HB20080214.ugp
and also
GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,cdf from the Affy source

I DID not recreate the monocell: GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,monocell.CDF

I'm at a loss to understand what I did to corrupt the objects on disk
-- or elsewhere...
i just can't figure what happened...

Comments pls.
Thanks
Chad Shaw

Just tried the full 'aroma.affymetrix' install script on a fresh R 2.7 and
'aroma.core' failed because it depends on the 'digest' package.  I
manually installed the 'digest' package from CRAN, reran and it worked no

Thought you should know.

Cheers,

The rule is that the last dimension/index (here 1:42) is always the
one corresponding to the arrays.  You can get the names/fullnames of
the arrays using getNames(cs)/getFullNames(cs), and they are in that
order.  [The array names are not added on purpose because the
memory/time overhead is too big].

messages.subject: limma analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I've got some questions about limma analysis with aroma.affymetrix (or with data generated by aroma.affymetrix).

Since there is no detailed information about FIRMA available so far (Are there any status-updates?), I would like to do a 't-test-like' test on the exon-level-estimates. The general outline would be as follows. The data is four HuEx-1_0-st-v2-chips per group (treatment/control). The chips are unpaired. So I could do a t-test for every exon (I would expect to do this on "core"-exons) and get around 18708 p-values (t-statistics). Then I could plot a histogram with 20 columns on the x-axis: column1 0<=p<0.05, column2 0.05<=p<0.10 and so on. If there is no difference between control and treatment I would see equally distributed data at a level of 18708/20 \approx 935. So any data in column1 above this level would suggest that there is something alternativly expressed. The amount of exons in column1 above the 'by-chance threshold' would give me a vague idea whether there is some alternative expression in my data (and I should invest more time for further analysis) or not. I also thought of volcano plots which could could give me exons with a low p-value and high log-fold change.

So far for the general idea. For several reasons a limma test seems to be appropriate for this. I know the limma package is well documented but as I understand it, some of you are quit familiar with this package and since there is so much to do wrong, I would appreciate some help very much.

Suppose I have done (the usual) BG-Adjustment, Normalization and Summarization already.
...
> plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
> fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
...
How do I continue from here? As far as I understand it, the essential step in the limma analysis is
> fit <- lmFit(eset,design)
> fit.eBayes <- eBayes(fit)

How do I "convert/export" the CelSet 'plmEx' from affymetrix.aroma to the 'eset' for limma? How do I setup the design model?

Could someone help me out with some lines of code or so? Or at least point out the relevant section in the limma user manual? Or maybe if you have objections concerning the whole approach let me know too.

Thanks a lot (again),
Frank

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] limma analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frank,

So I just finished some changes to the FIRMA paper which was holding me
back from putting it online, so I should be able to put it up soon.

In terms of the analysis you are suggesting, the main problem (if I
understand you correctly) is that you would just look for differences in
exon expression between the two groups. This will not pick up just
alternative splicing but also any differential expression at the gene
level (i.e. common to all exons within the gene). A better route, if you
want to go this way, is to take the affymetrix approach calculate what
they call the 'splicing index' -- the difference between the gene and
exon expression -- and look for group differences there. The SI will not
be zero centered and also will depend on the gene specific noise, so is
not itself easy to compare across genes. However, if you are doing a
t-test this would iron itself out.

To do this
plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
fit(plmGene, verbose=verbose)

plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)

exDF<-extractDataFrame(plmEx,addNames=TRUE)
exDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(exDF[,-c(1:5)]) #the first 5 columns are the names
geneDF<-extractDataFrame(plmGene,addNames=TRUE)
geneDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(geneDF[,-c(1:5)])

In prinicipal, you could then calculate the SI by subtracting from each
exon expression (row) of exDF from the appropriate gene (row) expression
in geneDF. However, you have to line up which exons go with which genes.
By choosing 'addNames=T', you will have the 'unitName' (the gene
identifier) in both dataframes so you can match them up (DON'T use other
output, such as 'unit', 'group' or 'groupName' since these will not line
up between the two data frames). I have simple code below (i.e. slow)
that does this given the dataframe imputs (on the log scale). Then you'd
just take that dataframe and create the necessary input (I think limma
will take just matrix too, it's quite nice and flexible). If you went
the FIRMA route, you could also do extractDataFrame on the firma object
and do comparisons (or even limma analysis) on that data frame.

Now I'm assuming you're only using 'core' exons, etc. These data frames
will not be unmanagable in this case (the exon around 300,000 rows and
the gene around 20,000 rows) -- I can do this on my laptop.

Note, that you might also want to filter based on the exDF. It will
actually be in the same order as the firmaDF you would get out from the
FIRMA analysis too, so the same filter could be used for either analysis.

Best,
Elizabeth

calculateSI<-function(geneEffectsDF,exonEffectsDF,skip=1:5){
     units<-geneEffectsDF$unitName
     if(any(ncol(geneEffectsDF[,-skip])!=ncol(exonEffectsDF[,-skip])))
stop("Matrices do not match")
     SIDF<-exonEffectsDF
     SIDF[,-skip]<-NA
     cumMatch<-NULL
     for(i in 1:length(units)){
         whMatch<-which(exonEffectsDF$unitName==units[i])
         cumMatch<-c(cumMatch,whMatch)
         if(length(whMatch)==0){
             warning("Unit",i,"is not found in the exon data frame")
             next;
         }
         geneEff<-as.numeric(geneEffectsDF[i,-skip])

SIDF[whMatch,-skip]<-sweep(data.matrix(exonEffectsDF[whMatch,-skip]),2,geneEff,"-")

     }
     if(length(cumMatch)!=nrow(exonEffectsDF)) warning("Some units in
exon data frame were not found in the gene data frame")
     return(SIDF)

}

messages.subject: Timings & Chunk Size
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

is anybody interested in the performance (not in a memory-bounded sense, but in a runtime sense) of the algorithms for BC, Normalization and Summarization and did someone do some timings?

I expected for instance that the plm-fit would take much more time for the "full-cdf" than for the "core-cdf". But surprisingly I observed that it's the other way around...! Reading and writing operations took nearly 88% of the time and since both operations work with the same "full-size" CEL file, I suspect that there is the same amount of I/O for both cdfs. Maybe this cancels out the effect, that for "core-cdf" less units have to be fitted (fitting took only about 8% of the time)!? But this wouldn't explain, why "core-cdf" takes even more time... Maybe my CPU had different loads for other tasks -- I'll double check it. Same effect observed for the BC by the way.

Another question came to my mind when thinking about the I/O of the algorithms: How is the chunk size determined? I had a look at fit.ProbeLevelModel and found that the minimal (fixed) chunksize is bytesPerChunk <- 1e+08 (100MB) and that the "unitsPerChunk <- ram * bytesPerChunk/bytesPerUnit" can be altered with the argument "ram" or "moreUnits" . But I didn't figure out, how to use this in the method call? And isn't there any way in R to determine the available system memory (like gc() or so) and assign a certain amount of it to the method. So you could run the same script on any machine (notebook, workstation, server) and always use the "optimal" amount of the system memory, which could avoid unnecessary I/O because of to small chunks.

This issue is not so VERY important to me, but maybe someone has experience with timings or knowledge of the latter problem.

Thanks,
Frank

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Timings & Chunk Size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Frank,

Can you send your code so that we know what you are talking about for
your steps (and how many arrays are you running)? For example if you are
doing mergeGroups=FALSE, the I/O will dominate (four or less probes per
fit); with mergeGroups=TRUE, you could have some long genes and the
fitting starts to take longer. Also, then the number of probes per gene
will vary dramatically. For example with one dataset when I did
mergeGroups=TRUE, 80% was spent fitting while with mergeGroups=FALSE it
was only about 25% -- and took less time (for the same cdf in both
cases). This varies by dataset, obviously. Ken ran some performance
evaluations a while back as to how the fitting step grew with more
samples or more probes and my recollection was that it was roughly
exponential in the number of probes, but I don't remember precisely.
However the process has been changed a bit so that by default with
really large genes (>500 probes I think) median polish is used instead
of IRLS to fit the model which significantly improves the time for
fitting the large genes. I wouldn't expect core to take LONGER, but I
guess if mergeGroups=FALSE I could see it being similar.

There are a number of previous conversations on related topics -- you
might try searching the previous discussions. It might be worth pulling
that information together, but it won't be something I do right away.

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: limma analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

Just thought I'd interject with a couple thoughts on this, given that I
had suggested limma previously.

If I understand your question, you are looking for differentially
expressed transcripts OR differentially spliced transcripts between your
two groups (Ctrl/Normal).

Personally, I don't like running limma or any statistical test for
differential expression (DE) at the exon (PSR) level.  The reason is
twofold: i) you pay a huge price in multiple testing (think ~200000
tests), and ii) if an exon is DE, you don't know whether it is actually
the gene that is DE or if it is differentially spliced (DS).

My feeling is you'd want to do a two-step approach: first, look at
gene-level DE (mergeGroups=TRUE fitting), then look at differential
splicing (i.e. FIRMA scores).  So, you could run limma on your gene-level
expression estimates to look for DE and you could run limma on the FIRMA
scores to look for DS (Note: you have to pay the multiple testing price
here).

A gene can be differentially expressed as well as differentially spliced
(and its not clear that we can always disentangle the two), but at least
these two steps give you an indication of it.

Either way, its always helpful to look at the probe-level data for the
genes/exons that come out as significant.

Hope that is helpful.

Mark

> of the FIRMA paper. And since a limma analysis maybe could be useful to
interpret the FIRMA scores (Mark suggested so some time ago) I thought
it
> could be useful to learn something about the limma package anyway. So
I'm
> still hoping for some hints about how to do a limma-test with the
plm-estimates (two, unpaired groups. moderatet t-test on the expression
estimates on exon or gene level).

Use fits <- fit(cbs, ..., .retResults=TRUE) where 'cbs' is a CbsModel.

>> [It's not "aroma" (different package) but "aroma.affymetrix"]
>>
>>
>>
>> > I was thinking of doing something additive to make all intensities
>> > positive but I'm not sure what effect this will have on the calling
>> > function.  Can anyone suggest an alternative approach?  Or, is there
>> > another calling package available that may work better with output
>> > from Aroma?
>>
>> So, in the bigger picture, downstream methods (that models the
>> logarithm of the signals) have to decide on how to deal with
>> non-positive signals.  Note that I write "non-positive" and not
>> "negative", because we might have zeros as well.  We should expect
>> non-positive in SNP data, because for genotypes AA and BB, ideally we
>> have all zero signals for Allele B and Allele A, respectively.
>> Indeed, 50% of the genotypes are expected to be AA or BB, so the
>> expected number of zero probe signals in also 50%.  Now, add noise to
>> this and it is not hard to imagine that the observed values are
>> negative as well.  If you assume symmetric noise, half of the signals
>> will be negative and half positive (for AA and BB).  Thus, typically
>> you see 25% negative (non-positive) signals if the calibration works
>> well.
>>
>> There are various ways to handle non-positive signals if you want to
>> pass them down to existing methods (based on the log transform).  One
>> can filter the signals such that all PM <= 0 as flagged as missing
>> (NAs).  An alternative is to censor the data such they are all set to
>> zero (or a small positive value).  Another alternative is to translate
>> the data such that less or no probe signals are non-positive.  The
>> advantage with the latter is that if you shift the data the same
>> amount for all arrays you know that you have the same systematic
>> effect in all arrays and multi-chip methods such as BRLMM (and CRLMM)
>> gain from that.  All these approaches are likely to give biases in the
>> estimates, but that might be the price you have to pay if you want to
>> use log-models.  Of the three, I'd say shift the data (but maybe you
>> have to accept some negatives in order not to shift too much), because
>> BRLMM/CRLMM should handle such data "alright".
>>
>> Having said all this, I would suggest that you post a message on
>> Affymetrix forum about adding support for non-positive signals in
>> APT/BRLMM, e.g. handling as missing values, censoring, or shifting.  A
>> genotyping software should handle such cases. They are good (and busy)
>> guys there and I'm sure they consider it.
>>
>> You can of course also shift the data using aroma.affymetrix.  There
>> is no ready class for this, but ScaleNormalization takes argument
>> 'shift' and then rescales the signals to the same average across
>> arrays, which is roughly what AllelicCrosstalkCalibration does, so at
>> least (to a fairly good I guess) approximately you could use
>> ScaleNormalization for your purpose.
>>
>> See also if you can use CRLMM in oligo. [It's on the todo list to
>> incorporate an aroma.affymetrix API for this, but yet to be done].
>>
>> Let us know how it goes - I'm quite interested in the outcome.  If
>> you're willing to write up a vignette or similar that would be great.
>>
>> Cheers
>>
>> Henrik
>>
>>
>>
>> > Thanks in advance.
>> > Andy
> >
>

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] error while executing AllelicCrosstalkCalibration
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Fri, May 30, 2008 at 2:03 PM, biobee <manis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am facing a problem at the AllelicCrosstalkCalibration step.
> I had loaded previously loaded a dataset of 233 .CEL files. Then I
> deleted all objects from my R session and re-started R with
> aroma.affymetrix. This time i loaded 145 samples. However, at the
> AllelicCrosstalkCalibration step, it seems to have info about the
> previous 233 files and hence is throwing an error.

Yes, this is the designed and intended behavior.  The main idea is
that if you use a different set of input files, you should use a
different output data set (path).  If the number of existing output
files does not match the number of input files, that is an indicator
of a potential error.

The quick solution to your problem to delete the output data set/path,
e.g. probeData/tumor,testSet,ACC,-XY/GenomeWideSNP_6, and rerun.

Your use case is quite rare.  You have delete CEL files in your
rawData/ data set, making it a different nature.  I would simply
rename that data set, say, by adding tag "145", e.g.

  rawData/tumor,testSet,145/GenomeWideSNP_6

That would solve all your problems.

>
> I tried to clear the cache by calling clearCache(.). But didnot help.
> Also tried  list.files(getCachePath("aroma.affymetrix")) , but didnot
> get to see the object.

FYI, clearCache() only removes things stored in memory, so that is
unrelated to what's on the file system.  What's in the "temporary"
file cache (e.g. getCachePath("aroma.affymetrix")), is also unrelated
to your persistent results in probeData/.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, May 30, 2008 at 3:02 PM, biobee <manis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> As a follow up to my earlier query on an unpaired analysis between
> normal (using this as reference set) and tumor samples, I have
> attached the commands that I am using:
>
> cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("GenomeWideSNP_6", tags="Full")
> print(cdf)
>
>
> #processing tumor samples:
>
> cs1 <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("tumor,testSet",cdf=cdf)
> print(cs1)
> acc1 <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs1)
> print(acc1)
> csC1 <- process(acc1, verbose=verbose)
> print(csC1)
> plm 1<- AvgCnPlm(csC1, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=
> +300)
> print(plm1)
> fit(plm1, verbose=verbose)
> ces1 <- getChipEffectSet(plm1)
> print(ces1)
> fln1 <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces1)
> print(fln1)
> cesN1 <- process(fln1, verbose=verbose)
> print(cesN1)
>
> #processing normal samples:
>
> cs2 <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("normal,testSet",cdf=cdf)
> print(cs2)
> acc2 <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs1)
> print(acc2)
> csC2 <- process(acc2, verbose=verbose)
> print(csC2)
> plm2 <- AvgCnPlm(csC2, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=
> +300)
> print(plm2)
> fit(plm2, verbose=verbose)
> ces2 <- getChipEffectSet(plm2)
> print(ces2)
>
> # Create reference set :
>
> ceRef <- getAverageFile(ces2);
> ceRef$combineAlleles <- ces2$combineAlleles;
> ceRef$mergeStrands <- ces2$mergeStrands;
> cesRef <- clone(ces2);
> cesRef$files <- rep(list(ceRef), nbrOfArrays(ces1));
>
> # "Paired" analysis
>
> glad <- GladModel(ces1, cesRef)
>
> Q1.Just wanted to confirm if the above commands are in the correct
> order for tumor vs normal.

Yes, that looks alright to me.  Note also Ken's reply that you could
also follow the paired vignette online.  Here you are preprocessing
the two sets separately, and there they are done together.  That will
of course give different results. You have to make a sensible design
which you want to use.

> Q2. Where do I execute the PCR fragment length normalization for the
> reference set?

PCR fragment length normalization is done on chip effects, so you have
to apply it to those before running the segmentation.  Please see our
paper H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation
and assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics 2008, for details on the CRMA model.

> Q3. Is it possible to run CbsModel of this type of unpaired analysis.

Yes, the CbsModel class handles data very similar to the GladModel class.

Cheers

/Henrik

Ok.

> each chip), four of the tasks (1,2,3,5) actually completed, but the

> 4: Exception: Could not create file path: reports/includes/images
> 6: Exception: Could not create file path: reports/includes/js/
> ChromosomeExplorer4
>
> Do you have any idea why I get this message?

The *Explorer write common files to reports/includes/ each "run".
They are always the same.  The clash is that your hosts try to
create/write the same directories/files at the same time (or when the
file systems have locked these).  In this case, I don't think you have
to worry.

> Why do only 2 of 6 tasks have this problem?

By pure chance.  Has nothing to do with aroma.affymetrix.

> Do you have any idea how to solve this problem?

Don't think it is a problem.  Just try the *Explorer and see if it works.

Cheers

Henrik

Hi,

I tried the code Elizabeth posted above and want to give some feedback.

First of all one small remark: extractDataFrame is a method of ParameterCelSet and so the correct code has to be:

...
> plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
> fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)

> cesEx <- getChipEffectSet(plmEx)  # newline here !!!
 > exDF <- extractDataFrame(cesEx,addNames=TRUE) # changes here!!!
...

Everything else works fine -- thanks a lot. But I think your function rather should be called "calculateNI" because whats basically done there is to calculate the log of the "gene-level normalized intensity" (see attachment "NI-SI.jpg" of the Affy Tech Report). I extended the function in a pretty quick and dirty way and now it calculates the SI between the (in my case two) groups and does an unpaired, two-sample t-test for every PSR. With (a very small subset of) this data I made a volcano plot, which looks pretty convincing (see attachment "volcano_simplescatter.png"). Could maybe someone run over the code at the end and have a look if I did somthing completely wrong?

Another thing, that I'm still not completely certain about is the unit-group-cell thing. I think, this strongly depends on the used cdf. So lets assume I did not use the Affy-cdf but instead  HuEx-1_0-st-v2,controlR3,A20071112,EP.cdf. So then the units would be transcript clusters/genes, right? And the goups would correspond to the PSRs/Exons, right? And the number of groups per unit would be an indirect measure of the number of annotation sources, right? For "core" this should be mostly more than 1... But what is "cell" than?

Another problem is, how can get "real" names for my transcript clusters? With "real names" I mean a name that I can query at www.ensembl.org <http://www.ensembl.org> for instance. Do I have to use "HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy.cdf"? Suppose I want to know the name of the transcript cluster with name "2315251" in HuEx-1_0-st-v2,controlR3,A20071112,EP.cdf. Can I look up this unitname in HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy.cdf or will I get mixed up? Although the U-Ensembl49-cdf has more units it is not guaranteed, that every unit from the controlR3-cdf is also in the U-Ensembl49-cdf, right?  <-- I'm a bit confused...

Frank

######
calculateSI<-function(geneEffectDF,exonEffectDF,skip=1:5,group1, group2){
    units<-geneEffectDF$unitName
    if(any(ncol(geneEffectDF[,-skip])!=ncol(exonEffectDF[,-skip])))

        stop("Matrices do not match")

    SIDF<-exonEffectDF
    SIDF[,-skip] <- NA
    SIDF[,"p.value"] <- NA
    SIDF[,"t.stat"] <- NA
    SIDF[,"SI"] <- NA
    skip <- c(skip,max(group2)+1,max(group2)+2,max(group2)+3) #cols for p.value, t.stat. and SI were added

    cumMatch<-NULL
    for(i in 1:length(units)){

        whMatch<-which(exonEffectDF$unitName==units[i])

        cumMatch<-c(cumMatch,whMatch)
      if(length(whMatch)==0){
            warning("Unit",i,"is not found in the exon data frame")
            next;
            }

        geneEff<-as.numeric(geneEffectDF[i,-skip])
        SIDF[whMatch,-c(skip,max(group2)+1,max(group2)+2,max(group2)+3)]<-sweep(data.matrix(exonEffectDF[whMatch,-skip]),2,geneEff,"-",check.margin=TRUE)
      for (j in whMatch){
            SIDF[j,"p.value"]    <- t.test(SIDF[j,group1],SIDF[j,group2])$p.value
            SIDF[j,"t.stat"]    <- t.test(SIDF[j,group1],SIDF[j,group2])$statistic
            SIDF[j,"SI"]        <- mean(as.numeric(SIDF[j,group1]))-mean(as.numeric(SIDF[j,group2]))
        }
    }
    if(length(cumMatch)!=nrow(exonEffectDF))

        warning("Some units in exon data frame were not found in the gene data frame")
    return(SIDF)
}

> Hi Frank,
>
> So I just finished some changes to the FIRMA paper which was holding me

>
> In terms of the analysis you are suggesting, the main problem (if I
> understand you correctly) is that you would just look for differences in
> exon expression between the two groups. This will not pick up just
> alternative splicing but also any differential expression at the gene
> level (i.e. common to all exons within the gene). A better route, if you
> want to go this way, is to take the affymetrix approach calculate what
> they call the 'splicing index' -- the difference between the gene and
> exon expression -- and look for group differences there. The SI will not
> be zero centered and also will depend on the gene specific noise, so is
> not itself easy to compare across genes. However, if you are doing a
> t-test this would iron itself out.
>
> To do this
> plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
> fit(plmGene, verbose=verbose)
> plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
> fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
> exDF<-extractDataFrame(plmEx,addNames=TRUE)
> exDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(exDF[,-c(1:5)]) #the first 5 columns are the names
> geneDF<-extractDataFrame(plmGene,addNames=TRUE)
> geneDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(geneDF[,-c(1:5)])
>
> In prinicipal, you could then calculate the SI by subtracting from each
> exon expression (row) of exDF from the appropriate gene (row) expression
> in geneDF. However, you have to line up which exons go with which genes.
> By choosing 'addNames=T', you will have the 'unitName' (the gene
> identifier) in both dataframes so you can match them up (DON'T use other
> output, such as 'unit', 'group' or 'groupName' since these will not line
> up between the two data frames). I have simple code below (i.e. slow)
> that does this given the dataframe imputs (on the log scale). Then you'd
> just take that dataframe and create the necessary input (I think limma
> will take just matrix too, it's quite nice and flexible). If you went
> the FIRMA route, you could also do extractDataFrame on the firma object
> and do comparisons (or even limma analysis) on that data frame.
>
> Now I'm assuming you're only using 'core' exons, etc. These data frames
> will not be unmanagable in this case (the exon around 300,000 rows and
> the gene around 20,000 rows) -- I can do this on my laptop.
>
> Note, that you might also want to filter based on the exDF. It will
> actually be in the same order as the firmaDF you would get out from the
> FIRMA analysis too, so the same filter could be used for either analysis.
>
> Best,

>
>
> Frank Ziegner wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I've got some questions about limma analysis with aroma.affymetrix (or
> > with data generated by aroma.affymetrix).
> >
> > Since there is no detailed information about FIRMA available so far (Are

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,

First of all, I would strongly recommend against using global variables inside functions, unless there is a really good reason for doing so.  It is very dangerous programming practice.  In fact, in your example, there isn't any need for global assignments at all so it would be best to steer clear of them.

You don't have to use sapply() (which is s-l-o-w) in your case - ordinary loop structures should work fine.  In fact I now notice that you did try using local variables and not using sapply - was your code anything like this?:

cbs <- CbsModel (cesCase, ces2)

for (j in 1:length(cesCase$files)) {
  rawCNsAll <- c()

  for (k in 1:23) {

      rawCNs <- extractRawCopyNumbers(cbs, array=j, chromosome=k)$cn
      rawCNsAll <- c(rawCNsAll, rawCNs)

  }

  stdev <- sd(rawCNsAll, na.rm=T)
  sdRecordCurRow <- data.frame(sample=cesCase$Names[j], stdev)

 write.table(sdRecordCurRow,sdRecordFnameTmp,sep=",",row.names=F,col.names=F,append=T)
  print(paste("j", j))

}

If not, could you please try this and see if you get the same increase in memory usage?  I have tried the code you posted but with random numbers instead of real output from extractRawCopyNumbers() and see no increase, and similarly, the code above does not result in increased memory usage with random numbers.  If the above still results in high memory usage then the problem may be with extractRawCopyNumbers() or with your setup (you didn't give us a sessionInfo() or traceback() - were there any warnings etc.?).

Cheers,

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

ok, now I see what your problem is.  So, when you call process() on
the ChromosomeExplorer, an race-condition exception might occur while
creating the reports/includes/ files causing process() to
interrupt/quit before it calls fit() on the GladModel and plotts the
results. Since the setup of reports/includes/ is "orthogonal" to the
latter, one could let the Explorer to ignore these kind of errors.

I've updated the Explorer class with a alpha-version method
setParallelSafe().  After installing the patch:

library(aroma.affymetrix);
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix");

call setParallelSafe(ce, TRUE) before calling process() on each of the
machines.  That will make the Explorer to ignore "non-important"
exceptions that may occur due to parallel race conditions.

Tech details: Note that it this is very much a quick-and-dirty alpha
implementation; a much better solution would be to use a mutex
mechanism handling race conditions, but that is current not available
in R.

Let us know if this helps

Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Frank Ziegner wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I tried the code Elizabeth posted above and want to give some feedback.
>
> First of all one small remark: extractDataFrame is a method of
> ParameterCelSet and so the correct code has to be:
> ...
>  > plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
>  > fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
>  > cesEx <- getChipEffectSet(plmEx)  # newline here !!!
>  > exDF <- extractDataFrame(cesEx,addNames=TRUE) # changes here!!!
> ...
>

Sorry, about that. You are correct, extractDataFrame needs to be on a
ChipEffectSet.

> Another thing, that I'm still not completely certain about is the
> unit-group-cell thing. I think, this strongly depends on the used cdf.
> So lets assume I did not use the Affy-cdf but instead
> HuEx-1_0-st-v2,controlR3,A20071112,EP.cdf. So then the units would be
> transcript clusters/genes, right?

unit,group, and cell are ALL cdf dependent; moreover, for the output of
the ChipEffectSet when mergeGroups=T there is only 1 value per unit and
it's stored arbitrarily under the first group slot, so it gets a group
identification which is nonsensical (which is why I said use the
'unitName' to match things). For mergeGroups=F, however, the
group/groupName identifies the probeset. For cdf distributed by Affy,
the unit and group are identical (except for some controls) and there is
no grouping of exons/PSRs into genes/TC. In my cdfs (e.g.
HuEx-1_0-st-v2,coreR3,A20071112,EP.cdf) they have been grouped and unit
refers to TrCluster. (I'm not sure why you are using 'controlR3' in all
your questions, which is only control probes, rather than 'coreR3' --
you shouldn't use controlR3 for an analysis of AS)

And the goups would correspond to the
> PSRs/Exons, right? And the number of groups per unit would be an
> indirect measure of the number of annotation sources, right? For "core"
> this should be mostly more than 1... But what is "cell" than?

I don't understand this question: for the coreR3 cdf (or any cdf
grouping the exons) the number of groups per unit is merely the number
of PSRs per transcript cluster. Which is more or less the number of
exons per gene (really there are more PSRs than exons). In the Affy cdf,
it's mostly 1 group per cdf. I don't understand how the number of
annotation sources comes in...

Cell basically refers to an actual spot on the array (an indexing value
for each element of data that could be stored in the corresponding CEL
file).

>
> Another problem is, how can get "real" names for my transcript clusters?
> With "real names" I mean a name that I can query at www.ensembl.org <http://www.ensembl.org>

> <http://www.ensembl.org> for instance. Do I have to use

> "HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy.cdf"? Suppose I want to know the name
> of the transcript cluster with name "2315251" in
> HuEx-1_0-st-v2,controlR3,A20071112,EP.cdf. Can I look up this unitname
> in HuEx-1_0-st-v2,U-Ensembl49,G-Affy.cdf or will I get mixed up?
> Although the U-Ensembl49-cdf has more units it is not guaranteed, that
> every unit from the controlR3-cdf is also in the U-Ensembl49-cdf,
> right?  <-- I'm a bit confused...
>

The unit names in 'coreR3' type cdfs are the transcript clusters. the
unit names in U-Ensembl*,G-Affy cdfs have units corresponding to ensembl
ids (but the groups are according the Affy PSR, which is what the G-Affy
means). So the group names in the two are both the PSR names, so they
are the same, but there is no (simple) relationship between the unit
names. There is annotation of Affy that relates TC to genes (though
sometimes TC involves more than 1 gene), but I don't know whether genome
browsers can look up the names of TC. I tend to use the Ensembl cdf
because I can quickly look up the names (with biomaRt) and plot with
GenomeGraphs the results. Also, genes with significant overlap were
concatenated into one unit, but otherwise overlapping probes were thrown
out in the Ensembl cdf, unlike the TC definitions.

Elizabeth

> p.value, t.stat. and SI were added

>         cumMatch<-c(cumMatch,whMatch)

>             next;

>         }

> On Tue, Jun 3, 2008 at 8:05 PM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com
> <mailto:epu...@gmail.com>> wrote:
>
>
>     Hi Frank,
>
>     So I just finished some changes to the FIRMA paper which was holding me
>     back from putting it online, so I should be able to put it up soon.
>
>     In terms of the analysis you are suggesting, the main problem (if I
>     understand you correctly) is that you would just look for differences in
>     exon expression between the two groups. This will not pick up just
>     alternative splicing but also any differential expression at the gene
>     level (i.e. common to all exons within the gene). A better route, if you
>     want to go this way, is to take the affymetrix approach calculate what
>     they call the 'splicing index' -- the difference between the gene and
>     exon expression -- and look for group differences there. The SI will not
>     be zero centered and also will depend on the gene specific noise, so is
>     not itself easy to compare across genes. However, if you are doing a
>     t-test this would iron itself out.
>
>     To do this
>     plmGene <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=TRUE)
>     fit(plmGene, verbose=verbose)
>     plmEx <- ExonRmaPlm(celsetN, mergeGroups=FALSE)
>     fit(plmEx, verbose=verbose)
>     exDF<-extractDataFrame(plmEx,addNames=TRUE)
>     exDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(exDF[,-c(1:5)]) #the first 5 columns are the names
>     geneDF<-extractDataFrame(plmGene,addNames=TRUE)
>     geneDF[,-c(1:5)]<-log2(geneDF[,-c(1:5)])
>
>     In prinicipal, you could then calculate the SI by subtracting from each
>     exon expression (row) of exDF from the appropriate gene (row) expression
>     in geneDF. However, you have to line up which exons go with which genes.
>     By choosing 'addNames=T', you will have the 'unitName' (the gene
>     identifier) in both dataframes so you can match them up (DON'T use other
>     output, such as 'unit', 'group' or 'groupName' since these will not line
>     up between the two data frames). I have simple code below (i.e. slow)
>     that does this given the dataframe imputs (on the log scale). Then you'd
>     just take that dataframe and create the necessary input (I think limma
>     will take just matrix too, it's quite nice and flexible). If you went
>     the FIRMA route, you could also do extractDataFrame on the firma object
>     and do comparisons (or even limma analysis) on that data frame.
>
>     Now I'm assuming you're only using 'core' exons, etc. These data frames
>     will not be unmanagable in this case (the exon around 300,000 rows and
>     the gene around 20,000 rows) -- I can do this on my laptop.
>
>     Note, that you might also want to filter based on the exDF. It will
>     actually be in the same order as the firmaDF you would get out from the
>     FIRMA analysis too, so the same filter could be used for either
>     analysis.
>
>     Best,
>     Elizabeth
>
>     calculateSI<-function(geneEffectsDF,exonEffectsDF,skip=1:5){
>         units<-geneEffectsDF$unitName
>         if(any(ncol(geneEffectsDF[,-skip])!=ncol(exonEffectsDF[,-skip])))
>     stop("Matrices do not match")
>         SIDF<-exonEffectsDF
>         SIDF[,-skip]<-NA
>         cumMatch<-NULL
>         for(i in 1:length(units)){
>             whMatch<-which(exonEffectsDF$unitName==units[i])
>             cumMatch<-c(cumMatch,whMatch)
>             if(length(whMatch)==0){
>                 warning("Unit",i,"is not found in the exon data frame")
>                 next;
>             }
>             geneEff<-as.numeric(geneEffectsDF[i,-skip])
>
>     SIDF[whMatch,-skip]<-sweep(data.matrix(exonEffectsDF[whMatch,-skip]),2,geneEff,"-")
>
>         }
>         if(length(cumMatch)!=nrow(exonEffectsDF)) warning("Some units in
>     exon data frame were not found in the gene data frame")
>         return(SIDF)
>     }
>
>
>
>
>     Frank Ziegner wrote:
>      > Hi everyone,
>      >
>      > I've got some questions about limma analysis with
>     aroma.affymetrix (or
>      > with data generated by aroma.affymetrix).
>      >
>      > Since there is no detailed information about FIRMA available so
>     far (Are
>      > there any status-updates?), I would like to do a 't-test-like'
>     test on
>      > the exon-level-estimates. The general outline would be as
>     follows. The
>      > data is four HuEx-1_0-st-v2-chips per group (treatment/control). The
>      > chips are unpaired. So I could do a t-test for every exon (I would
>      > expect to do this on "core"-exons) and get around 18708 p-values
>      > (t-statistics). Then I could plot a histogram with 20 columns on the
>      > x-axis: column1 0<=p<0.05, column2 0.05<=p<0.10 and so on. If
>     there is
>      > no difference between control and treatment I would see equally
>      > distributed data at a level of 18708/20 \approx 935. So any data in
>      > column1 above this level would suggest that there is something
>      > alternativly expressed. The amount of exons in column1 above the
>      > 'by-chance threshold' would give me a vague idea whether there is
>     some
>      > alternative expression in my data (and I should invest more time for
>      > further analysis) or not. I also thought of volcano plots which could
>      > could give me exons with a low p-value and high log-fold change.
>      >
>      > So far for the general idea. For several reasons a limma test
>     seems to
>      > be appropriate for this. I know the limma package is well
>     documented but
>      > as I understand it, some of you are quit familiar with this

>      > the 'eset' for limma? How do I setup the design model?
>      >
>      > Could someone help me out with some lines of code or so? Or at least
>      > point out the relevant section in the limma user manual? Or maybe

>      > have objections concerning the whole approach let me know too.
>      >
>      > Thanks a lot (again),
>      > Frank

messages.subject: aroma.affymetrix v0.9.3 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

aroma.affymetrix v0.9.3 with companion aroma.core v0.9.3 has been
released.  Several bugs have been addressed, more non-Affymetrix
methods and classes have been migrated to aroma.core, and some new
features have been added.  The complete change logs for the two
package are below.

Please update by:

source("http://www.braju.com/R/hbLite.R");
hbInstall("aroma.affymetrix");

All previously installed patched will be removed.

  is also returned.

  = cdf, ...) : No CDF file for chip type found: GenomeWideSNP_6', if
  the CDF was set to GenomeWideSNP_6,Full.CDF and no GenomeWideSNP_6.cdf
  file was found.  This was because readUnits() retrieve (x,y) information
  units, which requires affxparser::readCelUnits() to locate the CDF to
  infer the number of probe column in order to map (x,y) to cell indices.
  Now readUnits() get the cell indices directly using getCellIndices().
  Thanks Yue Hu for noticing this problem.

  getRawCnData() of CopyNumberChromosomalModel was too conservative. This
  caused it to throw 'Exception: Argument 'ceList' contains a non-
  ChipEffectFile: NULL' whenever multiple ChipEffectSet:s were modelled
  and one of them did not have data for one sample.  One of the redundancy
  tests for the 100K platform was updated to test for this scenario.
  Thanks to Lavinia Gordon for spotting this.

  getReferenceSetTuple() of CopyNumberChromosomalModel would
  return too few reference files if some arrays were misssing for
  certain chip types. Thanks to Lavinia Gordon for spotting this.

  chip type, cause an error in ArrayExplorer:s for tagged chip types.
  Thanks to Maria Traka at BBSRC in UK for spotting this.

  resistant against race conditions occuring when you run them on the
  same data set in parallel.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Henrik,
I've read in the archives of the forum that no GC-content
normalization was currently done in aroma.affymetrix, only fragment-
length normalization, and this is indeed what the code shows. I've
tried to look at the effect of GC-content myself but I can't find the
information on Affy website about the full fragment sequence, nor the
tsv file that aroma.affymetrix would expect. The only sequences that
seem to be provided for SNP6.0 arrays are flanking sequences...

But I'm curious to know: did your tests show that GC-content
normalization had no or only marginal effect? On what platform did you
try this?

Thanks,
Nicolas

> Hi,
>
> ok, now I see what your problem is.  So, when you call process() on
> the ChromosomeExplorer, an race-condition exception might occur while
> creating the reports/includes/ files causing process() to
> interrupt/quit before it calls fit() on the GladModel and plotts the
> results. Since the setup of reports/includes/ is "orthogonal" to the
> latter, one could let the Explorer to ignore these kind of errors.
>
> I've updated the Explorer class with a alpha-version method
> setParallelSafe().  After installing the patch:
>
> library(aroma.affymetrix);
> downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix");
>
> call setParallelSafe(ce, TRUE) before calling process() on each of the
> machines.  That will make the Explorer to ignore "non-important"
> exceptions that may occur due to parallel race conditions.
>
> Tech details: Note that it this is very much a quick-and-dirty alpha
> implementation; a much better solution would be to use a mutex
> mechanism handling race conditions, but that is current not available
> in R.

"computeCN" <- function(object, model="GLAD",explorer=TRUE, ...)

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] allele-specific vs total copy number
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

if you replace the argument combineAlleles=TRUE with
combineAlleles=FALSE the RmaCnPlm (or whatever *CnPlm you are using)
will fit an allele-specific model.  It will provide you with (thetaA,
thetaB) estimates (instead of total theta estimates).  Use
extractMatrix(ces)/extractDataFrame(ces), where ces <-
getChipEffectSet(plm), to extract the theta estimates.

Since none of the downstream methods/models (e.g.
FragmentLengthNormalization, GladModel, CbsModel, ...) supports
allele-specific estimates you are on your own after fitting the CnPlm.
 I know that Adam Olshen is working on an allele-specific extension
for the CBS  method.

There are no reports that allele-specific estimates from GWS6 should
be bad - to me that sounds unlikely and I don't see why it shouldn't
work.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Problem running GLAD with ChromosomeExplorer on Cluster nodes
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: Problem running GLAD with ChromosomeExplorer on Cluster nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christian,

the patch I provided was only for the very basic race conditions in
ChromosomeExplorer, but not in preceeding models/algorithms, e.g.
GladModel, AvgCnPlm etc.

The whole paralizing of aroma.affymetrix (and other computations) is
complicated and the only safe solution to deal with race conditions
like the ones you are reporting is to work with a semaphore/mutex
mechanism.  Such a solution is not available in R and until that it
available it does not make sense to put much effort to work around it
in aroma.affymetrix.  I don't think the R language itself will provide
this feature in a long time.  Instead I think "we" have to to create
"mutex" package that provides the necessary features.  The challenges
is to make such a package to work on all platforms and more
importantly be bullet proof.

FYI, I've looked into options like using RSQLite to provide the mutex
functionality, but unfortunately it turns out that SQLite itself is
not parallel safe and depends heavily on the underlying OS.  It seems
that the easiest solution is to have one dedicated server handing out
semaphores via a TCP/IP connection (opening and closing connections
are race-condition safe to the best of my knowledge).  However, such a
solution is not immediately transparent to aroma.affymetrix, so I've
procrastinated that path.  One can also work with lock files as
semaphores, but they are not bullet proof and there are cases where
two processes can lock the same file - it is better than nothing but
not safe.

To summarize, don't expect parallel computation in aroma.affymetrix
until there exist a well tested "mutex" package in R.

Cheers

Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] GC content normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

On Mon, Jun 9, 2008 at 6:35 PM, Nicolas Stransky
<nicolas....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
> I've read in the archives of the forum that no GC-content
> normalization was currently done in aroma.affymetrix, only fragment-
> length normalization, and this is indeed what the code shows. I've
> tried to look at the effect of GC-content myself but I can't find the
> information on Affy website about the full fragment sequence, nor the
> tsv file that aroma.affymetrix would expect. The only sequences that
> seem to be provided for SNP6.0 arrays are flanking sequences...

I think you are referring to my reply on April 8, 2008 to thread
'[aroma.affymetrix] UGP and UFL files?'.  Yes, I think you are correct
that the TSV files provided by Affymetrix does not contain
GC-content/fraction information.  I guess (because I don't remember
the details), I did get separate TSV files from "somewhere" (probably
Affymetrix) containing this information.  That file needs to contain
one column 'probeset_id' and one 'GC' where the GC is a fraction in
[0,100].  See the above thread for the content.  I could publish those
files for the 500K chip set online, but in order to do that I have to
find out who to ask for permission to republish [I put it on my todo
list].

>
> But I'm curious to know: did your tests show that GC-content
> normalization had no or only marginal effect? On what platform did you
> try this?

I did study the GC-content effect for the 500K chip set and concluded
that the (across-array) effect is rather small after correcting for
cross-talk (incl offset) and fragment-length effects.  See H.
Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics 2008 for details.  It is important to understand that
there is a GC effect, but after controlling for other things the
effect is the same across arrays so that it cancels out when you
calculate the relative signals.

I have not studies the GC effect on GWS6, but I don't expect it to be
much different because the same two enzymes are used and pretty much
the same set of (SNP) probes.

Cheers

Henrik

>
> Thanks,
> Nicolas
> >
>

> pos <- getPositions(gi,units=units)
> unitNames <- getUnitNames(cdf,units=units)
> theta <- extractMatrix(ces,units=units)
>

> The command "print(ces)" confirms that combine Alleles was set to
> FALSE:
>
>> print(ces)
> CnChipEffectSet:
> Name: Spellman44TrainingSamples
> Tags: ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300
> Path: plmData/Spellman44TrainingSamples,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300/
> GenomeWideSNP_6
> Platform: Affymetrix
> Chip type: GenomeWideSNP_6,Full,monocell
> Number of arrays: 44
> Names: A1, A10, ..., D9
> Time period: 2008-06-10 02:32:06 -- 2008-06-10 02:32:10
> Total file size: 1185.77MB
> RAM: 0.04MB
> Parameters: (probeModel: chr "pm", mergeStrands: logi TRUE,
> combineAlleles: logi FALSE)
>
> If it gives allele-specific intensities, then the matrix should have
> 2*(number of samples) columns.  I had 44 samples, but the resulting
> theta matrix contains only 44 columns:
>
>> dim(theta)
> [1] 36572    44

Your assumption (that the allele signals are returned as paired
columns) was wrong.  There are in total 24,513 units on chromosome 22;

> str(units)
 int [1:24513] 34464 34465 34466 34467 34468 34469 34470 34471 34472 34473

Out of these 12,059 are SNP units and 12,454 are CN units:

> length(grep("CN_", unitNames))
[1] 12454
> length(grep("SNP_", unitNames))
[1] 12059

...and 2*12059+12454=36572 rows.  Thus, the allele-specific estimates
are stored along the rows not the columns.  You see this better if you
use extractDataFrame(), e.g.

> data <- extractDataFrame(ces, units=units, addNames=TRUE);
> data[1:10,]
        unitName groupName  unit group  cell NA06985 ...
1  SNP_A-1970657         C 34464     1 68306       1235.4    ...
2  SNP_A-1970657         T 34464     2 68307       3232.4    ...
3 ...

So, group==1 indiciates allele A and group==2 indicates allele B.  The
groupName indicates the allele nucleotide.  For all CN units there are
only one group.

For your convenience, I've added an extractTheta() to the latest
version of aroma.affymetrix.  That returns an 3-dimensional array,
where the 1st index is the unit, the 2nd the allele, and the last the
array, e.g.

> theta <- extractTheta(ces, units=units[c(1:10,24504:24513)]);

Thus, for the SNPs theta[,1,] and theta[,2,] holds the allele A and
allele B estimate, respectively.  For the CN probes, theta[,1,] holds
the "total" theta and theta[,2,] is always NA.

Hope this helps

Henrik

No. With combineAlleles=FALSE the CnPlm estimates the *chip effects*

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] GC content normalization
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

a follow up on where to find GC-content annotation files:

Affymetrix provides tab-delimited annotation files specifying the
GC-content for chip types:

o Mapping10K_Xba131
o Mapping50K_Hind240
o Mapping50K_Xba240
o Mapping250K_Nsp
o Mapping250K_Sty

I couldn't find anything for neither GenomeWideSNP_5 nor GenomeWideSNP_6.

The data files are downloadable from Affymetrix' Support Materials
pages (e.g. "Mapping250K_Nsp GC Content Data, NCBI Build 36, TSV
Format"), which you find links to under the corresponding chip type
page on the aroma.affymetrix site via
http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web.

Cheers

Henrik

On Wed, Jun 11, 2008 at 12:56 PM, Henrik Bengtsson <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> On Mon, Jun 9, 2008 at 6:35 PM, Nicolas Stransky
> <nicolas....@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Henrik,
>> I've read in the archives of the forum that no GC-content
>> normalization was currently done in aroma.affymetrix, only fragment-
>> length normalization, and this is indeed what the code shows. I've
>> tried to look at the effect of GC-content myself but I can't find the
>> information on Affy website about the full fragment sequence, nor the
>> tsv file that aroma.affymetrix would expect. The only sequences that
>> seem to be provided for SNP6.0 arrays are flanking sequences...
>
> I think you are referring to my reply on April 8, 2008 to thread
> '[aroma.affymetrix] UGP and UFL files?'.  Yes, I think you are correct
> that the TSV files provided by Affymetrix does not contain
> GC-content/fraction information.  I guess (because I don't remember
> the details), I did get separate TSV files from "somewhere" (probably
> Affymetrix) containing this information.  That file needs to contain
> one column 'probeset_id' and one 'GC' where the GC is a fraction in
> [0,100].  See the above thread for the content.  I could publish those
> files for the 500K chip set online, but in order to do that I have to
> find out who to ask for permission to republish [I put it on my todo
> list].
>
>>
>> But I'm curious to know: did your tests show that GC-content
>> normalization had no or only marginal effect? On what platform did you
>> try this?
>
> I did study the GC-content effect for the 500K chip set and concluded
> that the (across-array) effect is rather small after correcting for
> cross-talk (incl offset) and fragment-length effects.  See H.
> Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
> Bioinformatics 2008 for details.  It is important to understand that
> there is a GC effect, but after controlling for other things the
> effect is the same across arrays so that it cancels out when you
> calculate the relative signals.
>
> I have not studies the GC effect on GWS6, but I don't expect it to be
> much different because the same two enzymes are used and pretty much
> the same set of (SNP) probes.
>
> Cheers
>
> Henrik
>
>>
>> Thanks,
>> Nicolas
>> >>
>>
>

On Jun 11, 8:37 pm, "Henrik Bengtsson" <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Christian,
>
> the patch I provided was only for the very basic race conditions in
> ChromosomeExplorer, but not in preceeding models/algorithms, e.g.
> GladModel, AvgCnPlm etc.
>
> The whole paralizing of aroma.affymetrix (and other computations) is
> complicated and the only safe solution to deal with race conditions
> like the ones you are reporting is to work with a semaphore/mutex
> mechanism.  Such a solution is not available in R and until that it
> available it does not make sense to put much effort to work around it
> in aroma.affymetrix.  I don't think the R language itself will provide
> this feature in a long time.  Instead I think "we" have to to create
> "mutex" package that provides the necessary features.  The challenges
> is to make such a package to work on all platforms and more
> importantly be bullet proof.
>
> FYI, I've looked into options like using RSQLite to provide the mutex
> functionality, but unfortunately it turns out that SQLite itself is
> not parallel safe and depends heavily on the underlying OS.  It seems
> that the easiest solution is to have one dedicated server handing out
> semaphores via a TCP/IP connection (opening and closing connections
> are race-condition safe to the best of my knowledge).  However, such a
> solution is not immediately transparent to aroma.affymetrix, so I've
> procrastinated that path.  One can also work with lock files as
> semaphores, but they are not bullet proof and there are cases where
> two processes can lock the same file - it is better than nothing but
> not safe.
>
> To summarize, don't expect parallel computation in aroma.affymetrix
> until there exist a well tested "mutex" package in R.
>
> Cheers
>
> Henrik

messages.subject_clean: Running GLAD on three separate normalization runs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

I'm trying to process multiple batches.
Two batches are tumor samples, one batch is normal samples (they are
not paired, but I have a large amount of normal samples).
I processed each using cRMA, where I used the following commands (on
each batch separately):

cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("glioma,testSet",cdf=cdf)
print(cs)
acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs)
print(acc)
csC <- process(acc, verbose=verbose)
print(csC)
plm <- AvgCnPlm(csC, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=
+300)
print(plm)
fit(plm, verbose=verbose)
ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)
print(ces)
fln <- FragmentLengthNormalization(ces)
print(fln)
cesN <- process(fln, verbose=verbose)
print(cesN)

I kept the data analysis of each batch (Normal, Tumor1, Tumor2) in
different directories, where the subdirectories of plm, acc and so on
were created in each directory separately.
Therefore my data structure looks like this
DATA/Normal/plmData
DATA/Tumor1/plmData

I now have separate cesN, and I would like to run GLAD, comparing the
two batches of tumor samples to the normal samples.
Each cesN object has a path, which I can see by doing getPath(cesN),
for example
getPath(cesN)
[1] "plmData/glioma,testSet,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/
GenomeWideSNP_6"

I think I need to change the path, so it includes the dir before I run
GLAD (so it will become "Normal/plmData/glioma,testSet,ACC,ra,-XY,AVG,
+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/GenomeWideSNP_6"). Is this correct?
If so, how do I do that? I tried searching for a command called
setPath(), but couldn't find it.

How should I merge the results from each separate normalization, so I
can run GLAD comparing the two tumor batches to normal files?

Thank you very much,

Uri David Akavia

I am assuming you have generated a ChipEffectSet and now want to do
some further analysis on the summarised data.  There are not really
any methods for doing this in aroma.affymetrix, but if you extract a
data frame with your summarised expression levels (see the Exon
Analysis vignette again), you will be able to pass these to a package
such as limma.  The best place to ask questions about limma is the
Bioconductor list, but if you explain what you are trying to do
(analysis of time series data, by the sounds of it?)  then I or others
here may be able to help.

Cheers,

Ken

Hi Henrik,

> I think you are referring to my reply on April 8, 2008 to thread
> '[aroma.affymetrix] UGP and UFL files?'.

Thanks for your answer. Yes, that's the message I was referring to.

> I did study the GC-content effect for the 500K chip set and concluded
> that the (across-array) effect is rather small after correcting for
> cross-talk (incl offset) and fragment-length effects.  See H.
> Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
> assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
> Bioinformatics 2008 for details.  It is important to understand that
> there is a GC effect, but after controlling for other things the
> effect is the same across arrays so that it cancels out when you
> calculate the relative signals.
>
> I have not studies the GC effect on GWS6, but I don't expect it to be
> much different because the same two enzymes are used and pretty much
> the same set of (SNP) probes.

OK, thanks. Yes, that makes sense. But the design of the chips is also
different in the sense they don't have MM. I guess it should be
possible to build a file according to the format you mentioned
earlier, in order to run the GC-content normalization and study the
effect. I will probably try that.

Best,
    Nicolas

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] Re: processing data generated by how-to in Exon analysis page
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ray,

I'm pretty sure extractDataFrame() returns values on the original scale, so you will need to take logs.

So it seems that you want to compare each of your time points (2 reps at each time) to the samples at t=0, presumably to see which transcripts change expression over time.  I would definitely use the limma package to do this.  You could define contrasts (t3-t0, t6-t0, t12-t0, t24-t0, t48-t0) if you are just interested in the different time points compared to the initial time, and fit these to find differentially expressed transcripts.  At this point I would direct you to the limma documentation (which is excellent) and the Bioconductor list, since we are starting to get off-topic for aroma.affymetrix.

Cheers,

Ken

messages.subject: Re: verbose<-Arguments$getVerbose(-8)
messages.body_plain:
On 26 juin, 13:03, Ray <Raymond.Robe...@ncf.edu> wrote:
> What does the -8 do in this function?
> verbose<-Arguments$getVerbose(-8)

Quoting Henrik in the thread "decrease verbosity":
The smaller number (-20 is smaller than -10), the more details.  So,
verbose=0 (or FALSE) gives no details, verbose=-1 (TRUE) somewhat
more, verbose=-2 even more and so on.   Think of the value as the
"threshold" that one has to overcome in order for output to be
displayed.

Best,
    Nicolas
